content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper presented a novel continual learning algorithm through two alternating strategies: regional isolation and knowledge integration. Although knowledge distillation has been previously explored for Continual learning, this method complements KD with architectural strategies.

The paper has made a few unsubstantial claims as indicated by Reviewer SQbA. There are a number of hyperparameters and the choice of these hyperparameters are not well defined. The paper could benefit from more experiments on more complex data sets.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: The paper makes a few unsubstantiated claims, requires more experiments, requires a re-org of the manuscript for clarity. The authors have not addressed the reviewer's comments too.
content.justification_for_why_not_lower_score: This is a paper to be rejected.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting: The reviewers had raised a number of questions, but the authors have not responded to these. Considering the lack of clarity, the paper is a clear reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new algorithm called SRII for continual learning. After a comprehensive literature review, it introduces the two components of SRII and then the full algorithm. The two components are regional isolation and regional integration. Specifically, regional isolation is proposed to reduce the interference between the learning of the new class and the retention of the knowledge of old classes, while regional integration is proposed to integrate the knowledge of the new class and old classes and reduce the recency bias. The experiments in the appendix show that SRII outperforms some existing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper's strength is that the proposed algorithm is new, and the experiment results show that it outperforms some existing methods in the field. It also provides ablation studies on the regional isolation procedure and the margin loss.

On the weaknesses, I would say the writing is the biggest weakness of the paper. Although I can understand the proposed method with sufficient effort, the paper needs substantial rewriting before publication. The aspects to be improved are provided in "Clarity, Quality, Novelty And Reproducibility." Another weakness is that the paper doesn't include a hyperparameter sensitivity analysis. There are many hyperparameters in the proposed methods: $\alpha, \beta, \delta, k, b, T, \lambda$. Among them, only $k$ and $b$ are mentioned to be selected by grid search, but how about other hyperparameters? Are they also selected by grid search? Specifically, to investigate the utility of the distillation loss, how would the performance change when $\alpha$ and $\beta$ change? I think the paper would benefit from answering these questions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of the paper needs to be improved:
1. The notation should be properly defined and consistent. For example, H and W are not defined anywhere. The dimensions of the variables (h_m, h_{m+1}, etc.) are also not defined.
2. The format of the formulas needs to be improved. For example, "${s.t. grad(\theta_{C_old}^t)=0}$" in Eq (2) is incorrect. The gradient is the derivative of the variable. A proper way to express what is happening could be changing ${\arg \min_{\theta^t}}$ to ${\arg\min_{\theta^t_{new}}}$.
3. Some grammar errors need to be corrected. For example, the last sentence of the main text: "we will explore also" should be "we will also explore."
4. The figures should be vector graphics. For example, Figure 6 is quite blurred even under the normal scale.
Also, how much computation is used compared to other methods? If they  all train for 100 epochs at each stage, I would like to know how the computation budget is distributed to different training processes (isolated learning, fine-tuning, etc.)

Inspired by the human learning process, the method proposed in this paper is interesting, and the empirical evidence of the method's effectiveness is strong. However, the quality of the writing has not reached the publication standards.

On the novelty of the paper, I would say the proposed method is quite novel, but I also want to add that I haven't done a comprehensive literature review.

The link to the source code is provided in the abstract. Thus, I believe the result in this paper can be reproduced (although it violates the blind review policy).

Some suggestions on the writing:
1. Properly define what BN stands for. BN is an important operator and is heavily used in the text but is never introduced.
2. I suggest moving the values of the hyperparameters for the experiments to the experiment section.
3. Consider compressing some sections or moving the related work to the appendix and putting some important empirical evaluation results in the main text.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes Sustainable Regional Isolation and Integration to solve the class incremental learning problem. Regional isolation isolates new learning processes to avoid interfering with existing knowledge, while regional integration introduces knowledge distillation and margin loss regularization terms to alleviate recency bias.
The proposed learning strategy is interesting and promising.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

1 The proposed method is technically promising. First, isolation and then integration helps the model increase their knowledge while avoiding enlarging the structure.

2 The paper is clear and easy to follow.

3 One two datasets CIFAR100 and Mini-ImageNet, the method performance is promising.

**Weaknesses**

1 To prepare for learning new classes, the capacity of the proposed method may be only half of the full model. Why not substitute the isolation part with another model B, which has the same structure as the original one A. During integration, using knowledge distillation, transfer the knowledge of two models back to the original model A and erase the parameter of B. In this setting, it is similar to using knowledge distillation to solve continual learning.

2 More and larger dataset experiments would be better. The main paper does not contain the experiment results. Only using CIFAR100 and Mini-ImageNet may not be enough to support the claim. CUB, Flower, and full ImageNet should be considered. Also, adding more latest baselines would be better.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Clear and easy to follow.
Quality: the method sounds promising.
Novelty: knowledge distillation idea is not novel, isolation part is interesting while may have an easy substitution (above).
Reproducibility: provide code.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the reviewer is curious about the previous questions and updates. Novelty is one important concern. What would be the difference between the proposed method with directly using two models and knowledge distillation to solve continual learning (weakness 2)?

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a method that simulates the brain’s ability to continuously acquire and integrate new knowledge. The method consists of alternatingly incorporating knowledge into isolated memory areas, and then consolidating new memories with old ones through knowledge distillation. The authors further use a margin loss to help alleviate catastrophic forgetting and recency bias. The authors claim significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods for multi-stage learning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths:
- The paper treats an important question: how can we build machine learning models that are able to learn incrementally without catastrophic forgetting? 
- The presented algorithm is novel (but in many ways similar to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.01349v1.pdf). 
- The authors release source code. While I have not run the code or read all of it carefully, the code appears to be of appropriate quality. However, the code to generate the figures and results tables is missing, as is the code that was used to evaluate other methods using the evaluation methodology that the authors chose. From where did the authors obtain the performance numbers for baseline methods?

# Weaknesses:

- The central claim from the abstract ("In all 5-stage and 10-stage incremental settings, SRII outperforms the baseline and achieves at least 5.27%+ average accuracy improvement.”) does not appear in any form in the main body of the paper, and is not supported in the main body of the paper (some support is included in the appendix). The paper would be much stronger if it included an "Experiments" section in the main body of the paper, not just in the appendix, especially since the authors advertise the empirical performance in the abstract. 

- The authors do not include a description of the experiments run in the main paper, and do not include a detailed overview of their experimental set-up in the appendix either. What training data is given to the model at what time? What is the model evaluated on? It is on page 7 that the authors first mention the term “knowledge categories”. This is unusual, given the the authors advertise performance improvements relative to the state-of-the-art in the abstract and introduction. See e.g. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.01349v1.pdf for a paper (on the same topic as the paper reviewed here) that includes an “Experiments” section that, among other things, introduces the dataset and task well. 

- The paper is hard to read. The proposed method takes multiple reads for someone to understand, even for someone familiar with related papers. This is partially due to the structure of the paper, but also because of details such as a garbled sentence in the abstract, or acronyms that are not introduced (e.g. “IS”). The "Clarity" section below contains some suggestions for how to make this paper clearer. Taking a step back, I suggest that the authors have a colleague who was not part of the research effort read the paper, and have the friend explain the paper. This can help identify points in the paper that need to be written more clearly. 

- The code to generate the figures and results tables is not being released, nor is the code that was used to evaluate other methods using the evaluation methodology that the authors chose. From where did the authors obtain the performance numbers for baseline methods?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
# High-level remarks:

- The paper is unclear in many places, and overall difficult to read even for someone who is familiar with related earlier work. This is partially due to the organization of the text in which the method is introduced, but also due to sentences that likely broke while copy-pasting, as well as because acronyms and terminology are often not introduced. 

- The authors release the code used to train their models, and the code appears to be good enough to reproduce results. However, the code to generate the figures and results tables is not being released, nor is the code that was used to evaluate other methods using the evaluation methodology that the authors chose. From where did the authors obtain the performance numbers for baseline methods?

# Detailed suggestions for improvement

- The abstract states that “[human lifelong learning] is mainly attributed to the human brain’s ability of partitioned learning and memory replay”. I would soften this statement a bit, and write something like “has mainly been attributed to”. 
- To use correct terminology, I propose to change “while regional integration introduces knowledge distillation and margin loss regularization term” to “while regional integration uses knowledge distillation and a margin loss regularization term”.
- The following sentence in the abstract is garbled: “knowledge distillation to transfer replay knowledge for alleviating catastrophic forgetting, margin loss regularization term to clarify the boundaries of new and old knowledge for alleviating recency bias. and margin loss regularization term to clarify the boundaries of new and old knowledge in regional integration, which alleviates catastrophic forgetting and recency bias”
- Limitation: the authors experiment with 5-stage and 10-stage learning scenarios. In human learning, however, learning takes place over millions of stages. Since the algorithm is inspired by the brain, it would be interesting to see how the algorithm performs in longer-term learning settings. 
- The paragraph beginning with “Human’s continuous learning capacity also benefits from the memory replay of the hippocampal system.” makes statements about the human brain that are stronger than the claims in the paper referenced at the end of the paragraph. 
- I would change “In conclusion, the domains of knowledge distillation and incremental learning have generally converged. ” to “In conclusion, the domain of incremental learning has generally converged on knowledge distillation as a key ingredient ”. This is more meaningful since knowledge distillation (e.g. of large language models) has evolved largely independently of (and not towards) incremental learning. 
- The authors use the acronym “BN” throughout the paper. Does this stand for “batch normalization”? It would be helpful to spell the acronym out when it is first used. 

- I do not fully understand Figure 2. For example, there are two boxes with red dashed borders in the figure. Both red boxes are attached to the same time step. The labels of the objects in the two boxes, are exactly the same, but the “BN weights” and “channels” objects look different. How can there be two different BN weights and channel allocations at the same time step? Could the authors clarify this? Also: why are all BN weights in one of the two red boxes black, but the channels are a mix of white and orange? Actually, I see different shades of orange, and no true white in the channels object of the top red box. 
- In Figure 2’s caption, what does “is proceed by the weights of the pruned BN layer” mean?

- In “. grad(·) = θ denotes the gradient of the convolution kernel weights is set to 0”, should it be “. grad(·) = 0 denotes the gradient of the convolution kernel weights is set to 0”?

- “After regional isolation is completed, the isolated knowledge of new and old should form a unified representation.” could better be written “After regional isolation is completed, the isolated knowledge of new and old must be turned into a unified representation.”, as after regional integration the isolated old and new knowledge in fact do not yet form a unified representation. 

- The authors write “Knowledge distillation was first adopted by Hinton (Howard & Ruder, 2018) and is commonly used for model compression and knowledge transfer” . This paper https://www.cs.cornell.edu/~caruana/compression.kdd06.pdf did something akin to model distillation in 2006 (the authors call it model compression), before Hinton’s 2015 model distillation paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531). Related, I am wondering why the authors cited (Howard & Ruder, 2018) here. 

- In equation 4, it would be nicer not to typeset natural language English text in math mode italics. 

- What does “with low training challenge” mean?
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper investigates an interesting problem, but is not ready to be published or accepted. 
- The structure of the paper should be changed to include the key experiments in the main body of the paper, and the paper’s readability should generally be improved (see “Weaknesses” above). 
- The central claim from the abstract ("In all 5-stage and 10-stage incremental settings, SRII outperforms the baseline and achieves at least 5.27%+ average accuracy improvement.”) is not substantiated in any form in the main body of the paper. 
- It would be helpful if the authors stated from where they obtained the performances of the baseline methods, and ideally published the code to generate these numbers (if the authors generated the numbers themselves).

content.title: An Incremental Learning Approach for Sustainable Regional Isolation and Integration
content.TL;DR: Sustainable regional isolation and integration contribute to incremental learning while alleviating "recency bias".
content.abstract: Humans are capable of acquiring new knowledge on a constant basis, while integrating and optimizing old knowledge without forgetting them. This is mainly attributed to the human brain’s ability of partitioned learning and memory replay. In this paper, we simulate this ability and propose an incremental learning network of Sustainable Regional Isolation and Integration (SRII). SRII consists of two phases, regional isolation and regional integration, which are iterated to achieve continuous incremental class learning. Regional isolation isolates new learning processes to avoid interfering with existing knowledge, while regional integration introduces knowledge distillation and margin loss regularization term, knowledge distillation to transfer replay knowledge for alleviating catastrophic forgetting, margin loss regularization term to clarify the boundaries of new and old knowledge for alleviating recency bias. Experimental results on the CIFAR100 and miniImageNet datasets demonstrate that SRII outperforms the state-of-the-arts to avoid catastrophic forgetting. In all 5-stage and 10-stage incremental settings, SRII outperforms the baseline and achieves at least $5.27\%+$ average accuracy improvement. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Wuziyi123/SRII.
